Embryonated eggs of Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua) contain an initial energy reserve of 2.1 J , which supports the yolk-dependent embryo throughout the incubation period. At a stable temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the duration from fertilisation to eclosion is approximately 10.7 days , a relatively brief developmental span that reflects the small chorionate embryo size. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, known as prolarvae, emerge from the chorion after this incubation at 7 °C and measure a total length at hatch of 0.42 cm , while the wet weight at hatch is correspondingly low at 0.0016 grams , a value derived from an egg diameter of roughly 1.45 mm. Following this emergence, prolarvae remain lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk nutrients. The total duration from fertilisation until the point of first exogenous feeding, marking the end of the endotrophic stage, is approximately 14.4 days [ab = approximately 14.4 days] at 7 °C [T = 7 °C], a period during which the mouth-closed larva undergoes organ differentiation before encountering its first prey under natural conditions.

Pelagic larvae of Atlantic cod experience a critical allometric shift during metamorphosis, which occurs after approximately 52.7 days  at 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. At this larval-juvenile transition, the total length at metamorphosis reaches 1.376 cm , while the corresponding wet weight at metamorphosis is only 0.00126 grams . The comparatively small size of recently metamorphosed juveniles reflects the energetic constraints of the planktonic larval phase, during which exogenously feeding larvae must locate adequate prey to sustain rapid growth rates. The thermal regime of 6 °C during this phase is representative of the waters encountered by wild ichthyoplankton in the Barents Sea and Georges Bank, where cod routinely experience gradual warming as they transition from pelagic to benthic habitats. Post-metamorphic juveniles then begin a prolonged period of somatic growth that may last several years, progressively occupying demersal feeding grounds. The achievement of this morphological transformation represents a major life-history bottleneck, as individuals that fail to complete the pelagic-benthic transition do not recruit to the adult population.

Gonadal recrudescence and the attainment of puberty in Atlantic cod are influenced by thermal conditions and geographic location. In the Barents Sea, 50 percent maturation occurs at a total length at puberty of 78 cm [Lp = 78 cm], although research by Thor (2010) has demonstrated that this length decreases substantially in warmer regions, consistent with the species' plastic life-history response to temperature. Spawning adults in this population initiate their first reproductive event at approximately 7.2 years after hatching [tR = approximately 7.2 years after hatching] at 5 °C [T = 5 °C], a comparatively late maturation schedule that prioritises sustained somatic growth before the onset of reproductive investment. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active females reached 19.9% [GSI = 19.9%] at 11 °C [T = 11 °C] during the spawning season. This high relative investment in gamete mass is characteristic of an iteroparous batch-spawning strategy, where individuals may spawn multiple times over successive breeding seasons without complete reproductive exhaustion.

The maximum recorded longevity of Atlantic cod in the wild is approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], though most individuals in heavily exploited populations rarely exceed a decade. Corresponding to this extended lifespan, the ultimate total length that cod can achieve is around 200 cm [Li = around 200 cm], with exceptional individuals documented from the historic Norse stocks of the North Atlantic. The ultimate wet weight associated with such asymptotic dimensions reaches 96,000 grams [Wwi = 96,000 grams], placing Gadus morhua among the largest gadoid predators in its ecosystem. Individuals of this size are apex predators, feeding predominantly on capelin, herring, and benthic invertebrates. Under optimal thermal conditions characteristic of feeding grounds, the maximum potential reproductive rate of a fully mature female approaches approximately 117,800 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 117,800 eggs per spawning event] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], representing a substantial fecundity per batch that supports the species' high recruitment variability. This daily fecundity is achieved by batch spawning, where females release multiple egg batches over the course of several weeks during each annual spawning migration.

Comparative analyses across gadoid species highlight the distinct life-history strategy of Atlantic cod, particularly regarding its large body size and delayed maturation relative to smaller congeners. The total length at puberty of 78 cm [Lp = 78 cm] observed in Barents Sea populations contrasts markedly with earlier maturation in warmer, more productive regions where food availability accelerates growth trajectories. Field surveys consistently indicate that the ultimate total length of 200 cm [Li = 200 cm] is attained only after many years of sustained feeding on energy-rich prey, and the corresponding ultimate wet weight of 96,000 grams [Wwi = 96,000 grams] represents a maximum achievable only under favourable environmental conditions with minimal fishing pressure. The gonadosomatic index of 19.9% [GSI = 19.9%] was recorded at 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. Finally, the initial egg energy of 2.1 J  places cod eggs at the lower end of the range for marine teleosts, yet the rapid development at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] ensures that hatching occurs before significant predation on the chorionate embryo reduces survivorship, underscoring the ecological trade-offs inherent in the early life stages of this commercially vital species.
